takeaway: AtomicDisk adds sync atomicity to TEE storage, letting recovery reject transient cache-eviction snapshots that are cryptographically valid but were never intentionally committed by the application.
background: A trusted execution environment protects code and memory from a privileged host, but persistent data still leaves that boundary. SGX Protected File System encrypts data and uses a Merkle hash tree and recovery journal for confidentiality, integrity, freshness, and crash consistency.
villain: The storage interface does not constrain when dirty cache blocks reach disk. SGX-PFS can therefore create valid intermediate snapshots before an application calls sync; a malicious host can capture and replay one of these states, such as a Redis configuration before its password directive was written.
approach: AtomicDisk defines sync atomicity: all writes preceding a completed sync become committed together. It marks eviction-written disk images uncommitted, retains old block versions in an authenticated journal until sync, commits by updating protected metadata and clearing the journal, and after a crash restores only the latest committed versions.
impact: The mechanism closes a gap between cryptographic validity and application intent without modifying upper-layer applications or file systems, and highlights that transient crash states become security states when an untrusted host can replay them deliberately.

evaluation.overview: The authors reproduce an eviction attack, count snapshots under five block traces, and compare microbenchmarks, trace replay, Redis, and BadgerDB performance.
evaluation.implemented: A roughly 5,000-line Rust secure virtual disk derived from SGX-PFS and integrated with the Occlum SGX library OS, plus a public attack-reproduction artifact.
evaluation.setting: Tests use a 64-core Ice Lake Xeon server, Intel DC S3500 SATA SSD, 256 GB memory with 64 GB SGX EPC, Linux 5.17, and 100 GB virtual disks with 4 KB blocks.
baselines: CRYPT DISK modeled after dm-crypt plus dm-integrity

results.text: Across five traces containing 8–49 GB of writes, PFSDisk creates 173,000–788,000 replayable snapshots, whereas AtomicDisk creates exactly the one valid snapshot caused by the trace's final sync.
The authors report that AtomicDisk and PFSDisk have comparable throughput in fio microbenchmarks and all five trace-driven workloads because both incur similar Merkle-tree and journal work.
For BadgerDB YCSB workloads, AtomicDisk reaches 50%–85% of CRYPT DISK throughput while matching PFSDisk; Redis performance is reported as comparable across all three disks.

limitations: The threat model excludes denial-of-service, access-pattern side channels, and whole-disk rollback; the latter still needs a trusted monotonic counter. AtomicDisk keeps journal versions until sync, so it can consume more space than SGX-PFS. The prototype is evaluated in one SGX/Occlum environment, and its Merkle-tree protection remains substantially slower than encryption-only CRYPT DISK on some microbenchmarks.
phd_group_signal: The paper exemplifies security-systems research that starts from an interface-semantic mismatch, builds a concrete exploit, formalizes the missing property, and implements the smallest storage-layer mechanism that enforces it. Its artifact and adversarial evaluation reveal methodology rather than advisor quality.

claims.text: The authors demonstrate that replaying an SGX-PFS snapshot captured before Redis's requirepass directive is persisted can start an SGX-protected Redis server without authentication.
AtomicDisk distinguishes cache-evicted writes from user-synced writes with a protected commit flag and an authenticated journal that retains old versions until sync.
